lessons.title: TSH and subclinical hypothyroidism in the fertility clinic
lessons.objective: Know whom to test for TSH under each guideline, interpret thresholds before and during pregnancy, confirm subclinical hypothyroidism before treating it and explain why ATA, ETA, ASRM and NICE disagree about levothyroxine.
lessons.closing: TSH for everyone under ATA, ETA and ESHRE; only with symptoms under ASRM and NICE. A first subclinical result is confirmed after 4–6 weeks; with TSH > 10 ATA says treat; persistent subclinical disease may be treated under ATA and is treated under ETA, but not under ASRM. Overt disease: levothyroxine, and before fertility treatment.

lessons.title: Euthyroid thyroid autoimmunity and fertility
lessons.objective: Decide when to order TPOAb, explain why levothyroxine is no longer offered to euthyroid antibody-positive women (TABLET, T4LIFE), plan their follow-up and rule out steroids, immunoglobulin and selenium.
lessons.closing: Positive antibodies with normal TSH: no levothyroxine (ATA 2026 and ESHRE 2022), TSH every 3–6 months and an early check in pregnancy. ETA 2021 still allows case-by-case treatment with TSH 2.5–4.0, but predates T4LIFE. No steroids, no immunoglobulin, no selenium.

lessons.title: Thyroid in assisted reproduction, pregnancy and preconception
lessons.objective: Anticipate the effect of ovarian stimulation on the thyroid, schedule TSH and levothyroxine adjustments in IVF and early pregnancy, know which gestational hypothyroidism to treat, prepare women with hyperthyroidism and apply the ATA 2026 iodine recommendation.
lessons.closing: On levothyroxine: TSH 0.5–2.5, check 6–12 weeks before stimulation and 2 weeks after the positive test; do not test during stimulation. In pregnancy, TSH > 10 is treated and mild subclinical disease after the first trimester is not. Methimazole to propylthiouracil when planning; 6 months after radioactive iodine. Iodine: 250 mcg/day in total.

items.title: Who gets a TSH in the fertility clinic? The guidelines disagree
items.core: ATA 2026 states that TSH should be measured in every non-pregnant woman presenting with infertility or recurrent miscarriage (GPS). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] ETA 2021 recommends screening TSH and thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPOAb) in every woman seeking advice for subfertility. [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]] ASRM 2024, by contrast, recommends testing TSH and T4 when there are signs or symptoms of hypothyroidism, including irregular cycles, rather than in all infertility patients. [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]]
items.body:
NICE NG257 keeps its 2004 recommendation: offer thyroid function tests only to those with symptoms of thyroid disease (1.18.12). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] The ESHRE unexplained infertility guideline considers TSH good practice in preconception care (rec. 27, GPP) and recommends no further thyroid evaluation if TSH is normal (rec. 28, strong). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] The ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss guideline recommends TSH and TPOAb in women with recurrent pregnancy loss (rec. 24, strong). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

In short: ATA, ETA and ESHRE (recurrent loss) test TSH in everyone; ASRM and NICE only with symptoms. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: Which guidelines order TSH for every woman with infertility, and which only with symptoms?
items.pearl: If you work with European or ATA protocols, TSH is part of the basic work-up; if you follow ASRM or NICE, you need a clinical reason.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 4 (p. 494): TSH in infertility, GPS. ETA 2021, R1: 1, ØØØO. ASRM 2024 (p. 774): B; moderate. NICE NG257 1.18.12 [2004]. ESHRE UI 2023 rec. 27 GPP and 28 strong; ESHRE RPL 2022 rec. 24 strong. In ATA 2026, “strong” means “should” and “conditional” means “may”; GRADE certainty runs from very low to high; GPS = good practice statement (ungraded, operationally similar to a strong recommendation).

items.title: TSH thresholds: preconception versus pregnancy
items.core: Before pregnancy and during fertility treatment, ATA 2026 applies the same definitions of normal and abnormal thyroid function as in the general non-pregnant population (GPS). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] In pregnancy it prefers laboratory- and trimester-specific reference intervals; if these are unavailable, it suggests a TSH of 0.1–4.0 mU/L in the first and second trimesters (conditional, low certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.body:
ASRM 2024 also recommends the laboratory cut-offs; if unavailable, it proposes 4.12 mIU/L as the upper limit for non-pregnant women and those attempting pregnancy, and lowering the limit by 0.5 mIU/L in the first trimester. [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]] ETA 2021 defines subclinical hypothyroidism (and starting levothyroxine) from a TSH > 4.0 mIU/L, or above the assay upper limit if that is higher; it notes that the commercial assays most used in Europe have an upper limit between 3.60 and 4.31 mIU/L. [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]]

ATA notes that free T4 assays differ widely, so it sets no absolute values, and that the same method should be used to follow each pregnancy (GPS). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: Without laboratory intervals, what TSH range does ATA 2026 suggest in the first and second trimesters, and what limit does ASRM use before pregnancy?
items.pearl: A TSH of 3.0 in a woman trying to conceive is not “subclinical” for any of these guidelines: the 2.5 cut-off is used mainly as a treatment target, not as a diagnosis.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 1 (p. 488): preconception GPS; 0.1–4.0 mU/L conditional, low certainty. ASRM 2024 (pp. 767–768): B; moderate. ETA 2021, methodology and definitions section. In ATA 2026, “strong” means “should” and “conditional” means “may”; GRADE certainty runs from very low to high; GPS = good practice statement (ungraded, operationally similar to a strong recommendation).

items.title: New subclinical hypothyroidism: confirm before treating
items.core: For ATA 2026, newly diagnosed subclinical hypothyroidism in a woman with infertility may be confirmed by rechecking TSH and free T4 after 4–6 weeks (conditional, moderate certainty), and fertility treatment may be delayed until it normalises (conditional, low certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] A TSH > 10 mU/L should be treated with levothyroxine (GPS). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.body:
The reason is that many women with an isolated high TSH have a normal value on retesting, and avoiding unnecessary levothyroxine spares anxiety, costs and the risk of overtreatment. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] If TSH normalises, TPOAb-negative women need no follow-up (seek care if symptoms appear) and TPOAb-positive women need TSH every 3–6 months while trying to conceive. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]

ATA accepts skipping the repeat when it is not pragmatic: time constraints from age or comorbidity, or a low chance of normalisation, such as a TSH > 6 mU/L or positive TPOAb; it then considers it sensible to offer low-dose levothyroxine straight away (25–75 mcg/day in the text and table; flowchart 1 shows 25–50 mcg/day) through shared decision-making. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] About 40% of women with subclinical hypothyroidism found in the infertility or miscarriage work-up are TPOAb positive, and 80% if TSH is > 10 mU/L. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: Per ATA 2026, what do you do with a first high TSH and normal free T4 in a woman with infertility, and when can you skip the repeat?
items.pearl: Order TPOAb with the repeat TSH: it decides follow-up if the value normalises and the shortcut if time is short.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 6 (p. 496): confirmation conditional, moderate certainty; delaying treatment conditional, low certainty; TSH > 10 GPS. The shortcut with TSH > 6 or positive TPOAb is expert opinion from the text (p. 497) and flowchart 1 (p. 501). Table 6 and the text give 25–75 mcg/day; flowchart 1 gives 25–50 mcg/day. In ATA 2026, “strong” means “should” and “conditional” means “may”; GRADE certainty runs from very low to high; GPS = good practice statement (ungraded, operationally similar to a strong recommendation).

items.title: Levothyroxine for subclinical hypothyroidism: four positions
items.core: ATA 2026 suggests, if subclinical hypothyroidism persists, low-dose levothyroxine (25–75 mcg/day) with a target TSH of 0.5–2.5 mU/L (conditional, low certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] ETA 2021 recommends levothyroxine when TSH exceeds 4.0 mIU/L or the assay limit, with or without autoimmunity, to keep it < 2.5 mIU/L. [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]] ASRM 2024 does not recommend treating subclinical hypothyroidism with levothyroxine in women desiring pregnancy or already pregnant. [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]]
items.body:
NICE NG257 found no randomised trials of treating subclinical hypothyroidism to improve fertility and made only a research recommendation on levothyroxine in women having fertility treatment. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] ASRM bases its position on levothyroxine not having been shown to reduce losses or improve clinical pregnancy or live birth, and on the favourable meta-analyses depending on one trial with data-integrity concerns. [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]]

The ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss guideline considers the evidence conflicting: treatment may reduce miscarriage risk, but the potential benefit should be balanced against the risks (rec. 48, conditional). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: What do ATA, ETA, ASRM and NICE say about treating subclinical hypothyroidism with levothyroxine before pregnancy?
items.application: Explain to the patient that there is no consensus: under ATA or ETA it is reasonable to treat confirmed subclinical disease; under ASRM it is not. Decide with her and record which guideline you follow.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 6 (p. 496): conditional, low certainty (row shared with follow-up after TSH normalises); the table and text give 25–75 mcg/day and flowchart 1 (p. 501), 25–50 mcg/day. ETA 2021, R12 and R13: 1, ØØOO per the summary table; the chapter text grades treatment without autoimmunity as a suggestion (2, ØØOO). ASRM 2024 (p. 774): B; moderate. NICE NG257: research recommendation 2 (2026). ESHRE RPL 2022 rec. 48 conditional. In ETA 2021, 1 = strong recommendation and 2 = weak or suggestion; ØOOO = very low quality, ØØOO low, ØØØO moderate, ØØØØ high. In ASRM 2024, strength of evidence is A (high), B (moderate) or C (low) and strength of recommendation is strong, moderate or weak.

items.title: How much does subclinical hypothyroidism weigh on fertility?
items.core: According to the meta-analyses and reviews summarised by ATA 2026, which include low-quality studies, untreated preconception subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH < 10 mU/L is associated in the general population with a slightly lower chance of conception (absolute difference −1.4% to −4.5%) and a slightly higher miscarriage risk (+0.4% to +0.7%), with similar figures in assisted reproduction. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] ASRM 2024 recommends counselling that subclinical hypothyroidism and a TSH of 2.5–4.0 mIU/L are not associated with more miscarriage. [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]]
items.body:
ASRM considers the evidence insufficient to say that subclinical hypothyroidism is associated with infertility. [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]] For treatment, ATA cites a single small, low-quality Korean trial (64 women having IVF/ICSI) in which levothyroxine improved implantation, miscarriage and live birth (miscarriage 33% versus 0%; live birth 25% versus 53%). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] ETA, reviewing the same topic, notes that a Cochrane review excluded another trial because the integrity of its data could not be verified. [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]]

For ATA, the plausible benefit of treating persistent subclinical disease is preventing progression to overt hypothyroidism, especially because ovarian stimulation and pregnancy increase thyroid demand. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: How large are the associations of subclinical hypothyroidism with conception and miscarriage, and which trial supports a treatment benefit?
items.pearl: Small associations in observational data and one 64-woman trial: that is why guidelines reach opposite conclusions from the same literature.

evidence.label: association
evidence.note: ATA 2026, section E text (p. 497). ASRM 2024 (pp. 770 and 774): miscarriage B, moderate; infertility C, weak. ETA 2021, IVF/ICSI outcomes section. In ASRM 2024, strength of evidence is A (high), B (moderate) or C (low) and strength of recommendation is strong, moderate or weak.

items.title: Overt hypothyroidism: euthyroidism first, then fertility
items.core: According to ATA 2026, every woman with overt hypothyroidism who is planning pregnancy should be treated with levothyroxine (strong, moderate certainty), and if overt hypothyroidism is newly diagnosed or uncontrolled, fertility treatment should be delayed until euthyroidism is restored (GPS). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] Liothyronine (T3) or desiccated thyroid extract should not be used in women planning pregnancy (strong, low certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.body:
In ATA's flowchart for raised TSH before conception, overt hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine at 1.5–1.7 mcg/kg/day. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] ETA 2021 recommends starting levothyroxine promptly in overt dysfunction (R11). [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]] ESHRE recommends treating overt hypothyroidism arising before conception or in early pregnancy with levothyroxine in women with recurrent pregnancy loss (rec. 47, strong). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

ETA describes the mechanism: in overt hypothyroidism SHBG and total testosterone and estradiol fall, prolactin rises and pulsatile GnRH secretion may be disturbed, with menstrual disorders in 25–60% of cases versus 10% of euthyroid women. [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]]
items.recall: With uncontrolled overt hypothyroidism, what does ATA 2026 say about fertility treatment and about T3?
items.pearl: If a patient on T3 or “natural thyroid” wants to conceive, ATA is clear: switch to levothyroxine alone.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 5 (p. 495) and flowchart 1 (p. 501). ETA 2021, R11: 1, ØØØO. ESHRE RPL 2022, rec. 47 strong. In ATA 2026, “strong” means “should” and “conditional” means “may”; GRADE certainty runs from very low to high; GPS = good practice statement (ungraded, operationally similar to a strong recommendation).

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman (fictional case), with no thyroid symptoms and regular cycles, attends after 14 months trying to conceive. Which guideline does NOT indicate ordering a TSH for her?

options.text: ATA 2026
options.why: It states TSH for every non-pregnant woman with infertility or recurrent miscarriage (GPS).

options.text: ETA 2021
options.why: It recommends screening TSH and TPOAb in every woman seeking advice for subfertility (R1).

options.text: NICE NG257
options.why: Correct: it only offers thyroid tests if there are symptoms of thyroid disease (1.18.12, from 2004, upheld in 2026).

options.text: ESHRE unexplained infertility 2023
options.why: It considers TSH good practice in preconception care (rec. 27, GPP).

items.explanation: NICE (and also ASRM 2024, which tests when there are signs or symptoms, including irregular cycles) limits testing to those with clinical features; ATA, ETA and ESHRE order it routinely.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman (fictional case) in an infertility work-up, with no age-related time pressure, has a TSH of 5.1 mU/L with normal free T4 and negative TPOAb. According to ATA 2026, what is most appropriate?

options.text: Start levothyroxine 50 mcg/day and begin stimulation that month.
options.why: ATA proposes confirming first; immediate treatment is kept for TSH > 10, TSH > 6, positive TPOAb or time constraints.

options.text: Repeat TSH and free T4 after 4–6 weeks before deciding.
options.why: Correct: many isolated high TSH values normalise; confirmation is conditional with moderate certainty.

options.text: Consider her euthyroid because TSH is < 10 mU/L.
options.why: A TSH above the limit with normal free T4 is subclinical hypothyroidism; the cut-off of 10 marks mandatory treatment (GPS), not the diagnosis.

options.text: Order TgAb and thyroid ultrasound before repeating TSH.
options.why: ATA leaves TgAb to physician discretion in selected cases and does not ask for routine ultrasound in this scenario.

items.explanation: If it normalises on retesting and TPOAb are negative, no follow-up is needed; if it persists, low-dose levothyroxine may be started with a target TSH of 0.5–2.5 mU/L.

items.stem: In a woman planning IVF (fictional case), TSH is 11.2 mU/L with normal free T4. According to ATA 2026, what applies?

options.text: Treat with levothyroxine.
options.why: Correct: subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH > 10 mU/L should be treated (GPS).

options.text: Repeat in 4–6 weeks and treat only if persistent.
options.why: Prior confirmation applies to lower values; above 10 ATA states treatment.

options.text: Do not treat, because free T4 is normal.
options.why: Normal free T4 defines the picture as subclinical, but does not exempt treatment with TSH > 10.

options.text: Start liothyronine for a faster effect.
options.why: ATA states not to use T3 or desiccated extract in women planning pregnancy (strong).

items.explanation: TSH > 10 mU/L is ATA's mandatory treatment threshold both before and during pregnancy; moreover, 80% of this group are TPOAb positive.

items.stem: A colleague tells you that treating subclinical hypothyroidism before pregnancy “is what every guideline says”. What is ASRM 2024's position?

options.text: Treat if TSH is > 2.5 mIU/L in women trying to conceive.
options.why: ASRM advises counselling that a TSH of 2.5–4.0 is not associated with more miscarriage; 2.5 is not a treatment threshold in this guideline.

options.text: Treat only if TPOAb are positive.
options.why: ASRM does not even recommend screening asymptomatic women for thyroid autoimmunity.

options.text: Treating it with levothyroxine is not recommended in women desiring pregnancy or pregnant.
options.why: Correct: it has not been shown to reduce losses or improve clinical pregnancy or live birth (B; moderate).

options.text: Treat all, because levothyroxine carries no risk.
options.why: ASRM lists adverse effects, misdiagnosis, costs and delays to fertility treatment from chasing a TSH < 2.5.

items.explanation: They do not all agree: ATA 2026 suggests treating persistent subclinical disease and ETA 2021 recommends treatment with TSH > 4.0; ASRM 2024 does not recommend it and NICE only calls for research.

items.title: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies: who should be tested?
items.core: ATA 2026 suggests that TPOAb may be measured in every woman with infertility or recurrent miscarriage (conditional, low certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] ETA 2021 recommends TPOAb in every subfertile woman and suggests adding TgAb if TSH is > 2.5 mIU/L with negative TPOAb. [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]] ASRM 2024 does not recommend screening asymptomatic women with infertility or pregnant women for thyroid autoimmunity, although it may be considered in recurrent pregnancy loss. [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]]
items.body:
ESHRE does not recommend thyroid antibody testing in unexplained infertility (rec. 26, strong), but does recommend TSH and TPOAb in recurrent pregnancy loss (rec. 24, strong). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

For ATA, TPOAb have better diagnostic accuracy for hypothyroidism than TgAb and, unlike them, are associated with worse reproductive outcomes; TgAb is left to physician discretion in selected cases, such as a euthyroid TPOAb-negative woman with a high-normal TSH and a high risk of autoimmunity. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] The prevalence of positive TPOAb in infertility or after a miscarriage is around 8–11%, similar to the general population, and perhaps twice as high with recurrent miscarriage. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: Which guidelines test TPOAb in everyone, which leaves it optional and which advise against it?
items.pearl: TPOAb does not change treatment of a euthyroid woman, but it does change follow-up: that is why it is ordered.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 4 (p. 494): conditional, low certainty. ETA 2021, R1 (1, ØØØO) and R2 (2, ØØOO). ASRM 2024 (p. 776): C; weak. ESHRE UI 2023 rec. 26 strong; ESHRE RPL 2022 rec. 24 strong. In ETA 2021, 1 = strong recommendation and 2 = weak or suggestion; ØOOO = very low quality, ØØOO low, ØØØO moderate, ØØØØ high.

items.title: Positive TPOAb with normal TSH: levothyroxine does not improve outcomes
items.core: ATA 2026 states that levothyroxine should not be offered to euthyroid women with positive TPOAb and/or TgAb and infertility, regardless of TSH or miscarriage history (strong, high certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] It relies on three high-quality trials: TABLET (NEJM 2019), T4LIFE (Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2022) and a Chinese IVF trial (JAMA 2017), in which preconception levothyroxine did not improve fertility or pregnancy outcomes. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
No factor modified the response, including a TSH > 2.5 mU/L, previous miscarriages, age or TPOAb titre; ATA takes this to suggest that the higher miscarriage risk is not mediated by thyroid hormone availability, and its mechanism remains unclear. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] ESHRE changed its recommendation in 2022, after TABLET and T4LIFE: euthyroid women with antibodies and recurrent pregnancy loss should not be treated with levothyroxine (rec. 51, strong, ⊕⊕⊕○). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

ETA 2021, which predates T4LIFE, suggests not systematically treating euthyroid women with autoimmunity undergoing IVF/ICSI (R19), but still accepts low-dose levothyroxine (25–50 µg/day) case by case if TSH is between 2.5 and 4.0 mIU/L before stimulation (R15), weighing age > 35, recurrent miscarriage or ovarian causes. [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]] That option no longer appears in ATA 2026. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: Which three trials led ATA 2026 to advise against levothyroxine in euthyroid autoimmunity, and which guideline still allows it case by case?
items.pearl: “She has antibodies and a TSH of 3, should I give her something so she doesn't lose it?”: under ATA 2026 and ESHRE, the answer is no; monitor TSH.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 7 (p. 497): strong, high certainty; dissenting comments are in supplementary material. ESHRE RPL 2022, rec. 51 strong ⊕⊕⊕○ (updated). ETA 2021, R19 (2, ØØOO) and R15 (2, ØØOO). In ETA 2021, 1 = strong recommendation and 2 = weak or suggestion; ØOOO = very low quality, ØØOO low, ØØØO moderate, ØØØØ high.

items.title: Euthyroid autoimmunity: monitor instead of treating
items.core: ATA 2026 suggests rechecking TSH and free T4 every 3–6 months in euthyroid women with TPOAb and/or TgAb who are planning pregnancy (conditional, low certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] In the trials, about 7–9% of these women developed (subclinical or overt) hypothyroidism within 12 months, mostly before pregnancy but also during it. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.body:
Euthyroid autoimmunity is associated with more miscarriage (absolute difference around +2% to +8% versus TPOAb-negative women) and with postpartum thyroiditis, which can also follow a miscarriage. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] Once pregnant, ESHRE states that TSH should be checked in early pregnancy (7–9 weeks) in women with autoimmunity and recurrent pregnancy loss, and hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine (rec. 50, GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

ATA suggests that antibodies may reflect a more general susceptibility to autoimmunity, but there are no data to support dietary interventions or immune-modulating drugs to improve outcomes. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: How often does ATA check TSH in a euthyroid TPOAb-positive woman trying to conceive, and what hypothyroidism risk justifies it?
items.application: Agree with the patient on a TSH every 3–6 months while trying to conceive and an early one once pregnancy is confirmed; explain that the risk of hypothyroidism is low but real.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 7 (p. 497) and text (p. 498): conditional, low certainty. ESHRE RPL 2022, rec. 50 GPP. In ATA 2026, “strong” means “should” and “conditional” means “may”; GRADE certainty runs from very low to high; GPS = good practice statement (ungraded, operationally similar to a strong recommendation).

items.title: Steroids, immunoglobulin and selenium for antibodies: no
items.core: ATA 2026 states that oral prednisolone or intravenous immunoglobulin should not be offered to women with TPOAb and/or TgAb and infertility (conditional, low certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] In euthyroid antibody-positive pregnant women, it advises against selenium supplements (conditional, moderate certainty) and against glucocorticoids or immunoglobulin (conditional, low certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.body: ATA's text summarises that there are no data supporting glucocorticoids, intravenous immunoglobulin or selenium to improve obstetric outcomes or lower the risk of hypothyroidism in pregnancy. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] ETA 2021 considers that understanding whether antibodies are an epiphenomenon of a general immune disorder would help determine whether treatments other than levothyroxine could improve assisted reproduction outcomes; it frames this as a research question, not a recommendation. [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]]
items.recall: What does ATA 2026 say about prednisolone, immunoglobulin and selenium in women with thyroid antibodies?
items.pearl: Selenium “to lower the antibodies” before or during pregnancy has no support from ATA 2026.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 7 (p. 497): prednisolone/immunoglobulin conditional, low certainty; Recommendations Table 11 (p. 504): selenium conditional, moderate certainty; glucocorticoids/immunoglobulin conditional, low certainty. In ATA 2026, “strong” means “should” and “conditional” means “may”; GRADE certainty runs from very low to high; GPS = good practice statement (ungraded, operationally similar to a strong recommendation).

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman (fictional case) is about to start IVF. TSH 2.9 mU/L, normal free T4, positive TPOAb. According to ATA 2026, what is most appropriate?

options.text: Levothyroxine 25 mcg/day to bring TSH below 2.5.
options.why: That is ETA 2021's case-by-case option (R15); ATA 2026 states not to treat, regardless of TSH.

options.text: No levothyroxine, and monitor thyroid function.
options.why: Correct: do not offer levothyroxine (strong, high certainty); TSH and free T4 every 3–6 months while trying to conceive.

options.text: Low-dose prednisolone around transfer.
options.why: ATA states not to offer oral prednisolone or immunoglobulin to antibody-positive women with infertility.

options.text: Delay IVF until the antibodies become negative.
options.why: None of the guidelines reviewed makes IVF conditional on antibodies; with euthyroidism there is no reason to delay it.

items.explanation: Three high-quality trials (TABLET, T4LIFE and the Chinese IVF trial) showed no benefit, including with TSH > 2.5; ESHRE agrees for recurrent pregnancy loss.

items.stem: Which document still suggests low-dose levothyroxine, case by case, in women with thyroid autoimmunity and TSH between 2.5 and 4.0 before ovarian stimulation?

options.text: ATA 2026
options.why: It states not to offer levothyroxine to euthyroid antibody-positive women, regardless of TSH (strong, high certainty).

options.text: ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss 2022
options.why: It recommends not treating euthyroid antibody-positive women with recurrent loss (rec. 51, strong).

options.text: ETA 2021
options.why: Correct: R15 suggests 25–50 µg/day case by case (2, ØØOO), weighing age > 35, recurrent miscarriage or ovarian causes.

options.text: ASRM 2024
options.why: It recommends neither treating subclinical hypothyroidism nor screening asymptomatic women for autoimmunity.

items.explanation: ETA 2021 already cited TABLET and the Chinese IVF trial, but it was published before T4LIFE and before ATA 2026, which the European Thyroid Association itself endorses. It is the specific European assisted-reproduction guideline, but on this point it has been overtaken by the later evidence cited by ATA and ESHRE.

items.stem: An 8-week pregnant woman (fictional case), euthyroid with positive TPOAb, asks whether she should take selenium. According to ATA 2026:

options.text: Yes, 200 µg/day reduces postpartum thyroiditis.
options.why: ATA gives neither that dose nor that benefit; it advises against selenium in this group.

options.text: Do not offer selenium supplements.
options.why: Correct: conditional recommendation, moderate certainty (Recommendations Table 11).

options.text: Only if TPOAb exceed ten times the limit.
options.why: ATA sets no titre threshold for selenium.

options.text: Replace selenium with low-dose levothyroxine.
options.why: Levothyroxine is not offered to euthyroid antibody-positive pregnant women either (strong, high certainty).

items.explanation: TSH monitoring is what ATA proposes for these women; neither selenium, nor levothyroxine, nor immunomodulators have shown benefit.

items.title: Ovarian stimulation and the thyroid: more estradiol, more TBG, more TSH
items.core: ETA 2021 explains that ovarian stimulation raises estradiol to 4,000–6,000 ng/L, as in the second half of pregnancy; TBG rises, free hormone falls and TSH rises. [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]] In about 1 in 3 euthyroid women TSH exceeds 2.5 mIU/L during the cycle, and the rise can last 1–3 months; it is greater in treated hypothyroid women. [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]]
items.body:
The guidelines disagree on TPOAb: ETA describes higher TSH and lower free T4 during stimulation in TPOAb-positive women; ATA 2026 states that in euthyroid women TSH during stimulation is comparable with or without TPOAb. [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]] [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]

Because of these changes, ATA considers it sensible not to order thyroid tests during stimulation or within 2 weeks of the ovulation trigger. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] It also warns that GnRH analogues or a miscarriage can trigger painless thyroiditis or Graves' disease, so tests should be ordered if thyrotoxic symptoms appear during treatment. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: Why does TSH rise with ovarian stimulation, and when does ATA advise not measuring it?

evidence.label: mechanistic
evidence.note: ETA 2021, “Thyroid Function and OS” section (physiology and observational studies). ATA 2026, Box 2 (p. 496) and text (p. 497): practical considerations, not graded recommendations.

items.title: On levothyroxine and having IVF: TSH target and timing
items.core: For women with infertility or recurrent miscarriage taking levothyroxine, ATA 2026 sets a TSH target of 0.5–2.5 mU/L before and during pregnancy (GPS). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] It suggests checking TSH once within the 6–12 weeks before stimulation, about 2 weeks after a positive pregnancy test and then according to pregnancy follow-up (conditional, low certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.body:
ETA 2021 recommends adjusting the dose before stimulation to keep TSH < 2.5 mIU/L (R14) and checking TSH after stimulation in women with autoimmunity on levothyroxine, on the day of the second β-hCG if pregnant (R17); it does not recommend this check in euthyroid women without autoimmunity who are not on levothyroxine (R18). [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]]

Most women on levothyroxine for overt hypothyroidism need a dose increase of about 25% by week 12 and 50% by week 20; ATA allows raising it on confirming pregnancy, by increasing the daily dose or adding two daily doses per week, taking the previous TSH and dose into account to avoid overtreatment. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] Then, TSH every 4 weeks in the first half, at least once in the third trimester and 4–6 weeks after each adjustment (conditional, moderate certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] In subclinical hypothyroidism diagnosed before pregnancy there are no data for that standard 25% increase; a small increase or TSH-guided adjustment suffices. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: In a woman on levothyroxine going for IVF, what TSH target and what check points does ATA 2026 propose?
items.pearl: Estrogen from stimulation brings forward the rise in levothyroxine needs compared with a spontaneous pregnancy: anticipate it.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 4 (p. 494): target GPS, checks conditional, low certainty; Recommendations Table 2 (p. 489): pregnancy checks conditional, moderate certainty; dose adjustment in the text (p. 501). ETA 2021: R14 (1, ØØOO), R17 and R18 (1, ØØØO). In ETA 2021, 1 = strong recommendation and 2 = weak or suggestion; ØOOO = very low quality, ØØOO low, ØØØO moderate, ØØØØ high.

items.title: Hypothyroidism found in pregnancy: what to treat and what not
items.core: ATA 2026 states that profound subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH > 10 mU/L) in pregnancy should be treated with levothyroxine (GPS); mild disease diagnosed in the first trimester may be treated (conditional, low certainty), and mild disease diagnosed after the first trimester should not be treated, with a repeat TSH after 4–6 weeks (strong, high certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] Overt hypothyroidism with TSH ≥ 6 mU/L, or persisting on retesting, should be treated (strong, moderate certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.body:
If new-onset overt hypothyroidism has a TSH < 6 mU/L, ATA suggests confirming it within 3 weeks before treating (conditional, low certainty); on levothyroxine it suggests a TSH within the normal range but below 2.5 mU/L, and in pregnancy only levothyroxine, never T3 or desiccated extract (strong). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] ASRM 2024, by contrast, does not recommend treating subclinical hypothyroidism with levothyroxine in pregnant women. [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]]

In recurrent pregnancy loss, ESHRE states that if a woman with subclinical hypothyroidism becomes pregnant again, TSH should be checked at 7–9 weeks and hypothyroidism treated (rec. 49, GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: Per ATA 2026, when is subclinical hypothyroidism found in pregnancy treated, and when not?

rows.text: High TSH in pregnancy, normal free T4 (ATA 2026)
Mild in the first trimester → levothyroxine may be considered (conditional)
Mild after the first trimester → do not treat; TSH after 4–6 weeks (strong)

visual.alt: Diagram: per ATA 2026, subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy is treated if TSH is > 10 mU/L, may be treated if mild in the first trimester and is not treated if mild after the first trimester.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 9 (p. 499) and Table 10 (p. 502). ASRM 2024 (p. 774): B; moderate. ESHRE RPL 2022, rec. 49 GPP. ATA defines trimesters pragmatically and allows shifting the cut-off by a few weeks. In ATA 2026, “strong” means “should” and “conditional” means “may”; GRADE certainty runs from very low to high; GPS = good practice statement (ungraded, operationally similar to a strong recommendation).

items.title: Hyperthyroidism and the wish to conceive
items.core: In women with infertility, ATA 2026 states that subclinical hyperthyroidism should be confirmed by rechecking TSH and free T4 after 4–6 weeks, and overt hyperthyroidism treated before conception, according to its cause or with low-dose antithyroid drugs if none is found (both GPS). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] Women taking methimazole should switch to propylthiouracil if planning pregnancy (strong, moderate certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.body:
If radioactive iodine is given for Graves' disease before pregnancy, ATA advises deferring pregnancy for at least six months. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] If only oocyte or embryo cryopreservation is planned with no transfer soon, antithyroid drugs can be continued during preservation. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]

ETA 2021 states that a subfertile woman with hyperthyroidism planning assisted reproduction should be informed of the higher risk of maternal and fetal complications, and that euthyroidism should be restored and maintained for several months before treatment. [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]]
items.recall: Which antithyroid drug does ATA 2026 recommend for women planning pregnancy, and how long to wait after radioactive iodine?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 8 (p. 498): GPS; Recommendations Table 14 (p. 510): switch to propylthiouracil strong, moderate certainty; radioactive iodine in the text (p. 510). ETA 2021: abstract (ungraded). In ATA 2026, “strong” means “should” and “conditional” means “may”; GRADE certainty runs from very low to high; GPS = good practice statement (ungraded, operationally similar to a strong recommendation).

items.title: Iodine before and during pregnancy per ATA 2026
items.core: ATA 2026 recommends that pregnant and breastfeeding women aim for a daily iodine intake of 250 mcg, from diet plus supplements as needed (strong, moderate certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] In women at risk of deficiency because of geographic region, dietary restrictions or malabsorption, it suggests a 150 mcg/day supplement, ideally from at least 3 months before pregnancy until breastfeeding ends (conditional, moderate certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.body:
It suggests applying the same recommendations to pregnant women on antithyroid drugs or levothyroxine (conditional, low certainty), and avoiding sustained intake or supplements above 500 mcg/day in pregnancy (strong, moderate certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] The accompanying text goes beyond the table and proposes advising 150 mcg/day to all women before conception, in pregnancy and in lactation, unless intake is high from dietary habits, noting that strategies vary by region. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]

The guideline gives no data on iodine status in Argentina or Spain: the regional decision depends on local population data that these sources do not provide. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: What total iodine intake does ATA 2026 recommend in pregnancy, to whom does it suggest 150 mcg/day, and what ceiling does it set?
items.pearl: Taking levothyroxine does not exempt from iodine: ATA 2026 suggests applying the same recommendation.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 3 (p. 491) and text (pp. 493–494). The table (graded recommendation) restricts the 150 mcg suggestion to women at risk of deficiency; the text extends it to all. In ATA 2026, “strong” means “should” and “conditional” means “may”; GRADE certainty runs from very low to high; GPS = good practice statement (ungraded, operationally similar to a strong recommendation).

items.stem: A woman with hypothyroidism on levothyroxine (fictional case) will start stimulation in 2 months. According to ATA 2026, what is the most appropriate TSH plan?

options.text: One TSH within the 6–12 weeks before stimulation and another about 2 weeks after a positive pregnancy test.
options.why: Correct: that is the Recommendations Table 4 schedule (conditional, low certainty), with a 0.5–2.5 mU/L target.

options.text: Weekly TSH during stimulation to adjust the dose.
options.why: ATA considers it sensible not to test thyroid function during stimulation or within 2 weeks of the trigger.

options.text: No testing until the 12-week scan.
options.why: Too late: levothyroxine needs rise early, especially after stimulation.

options.text: Target TSH < 4.0 mU/L before stimulation.
options.why: For women with infertility on levothyroxine, ATA sets 0.5–2.5 mU/L (GPS) and ETA < 2.5.

items.explanation: Estradiol from stimulation raises TBG and levothyroxine needs earlier than in a spontaneous pregnancy; hence the check 2 weeks after the positive test.

items.stem: Six days after the ovulation trigger, a euthyroid antibody-negative patient (fictional case) asks to “check her thyroid” because she feels tired. What is most consistent with ATA 2026 and ETA 2021?

options.text: Order TSH now and start levothyroxine if above 2.5.
options.why: A TSH > 2.5 is common after stimulation in euthyroid women and is not an indication for treatment; ETA does not recommend treating euthyroid women without autoimmunity (R16).

options.text: Avoid routine thyroid tests at this point, unless there are thyrotoxic symptoms or another clinical suspicion.
options.why: Correct: ATA advises against testing within 2 weeks of the trigger and ETA does not recommend TSH monitoring after stimulation in euthyroid women without autoimmunity or levothyroxine (R18).

options.text: Order reverse T3 to assess peripheral conversion.
options.why: None of the guidelines reviewed uses reverse T3 in this setting.

options.text: Order TPOAb and TgAb to decide on levothyroxine.
options.why: She is already known to be negative; and in euthyroid antibody-positive women ATA does not offer levothyroxine.

items.explanation: Stimulation transiently alters TSH and free T4; testing at that point confuses more than it clarifies, unless there are thyrotoxic symptoms, which ATA does say to investigate.

items.stem: In an 18-week pregnant woman (fictional case), a mildly raised TSH with normal free T4 is found, with no known TPOAb. According to ATA 2026, what applies?

options.text: Low-dose levothyroxine to protect neurodevelopment.
options.why: After the first trimester, ATA states that levothyroxine should not be offered for mild subclinical disease (strong, high certainty).

options.text: Do not offer levothyroxine and repeat TSH after 4–6 weeks.
options.why: Correct: strong recommendation with high certainty (Recommendations Table 10).

options.text: Levothyroxine only if TSH is > 4.0 mU/L.
options.why: The threshold that mandates treatment in pregnancy is TSH > 10 mU/L, not 4.0.

options.text: Selenium supplement and postpartum check.
options.why: ATA does not propose selenium in pregnancy; the indicated check is a repeat TSH after 4–6 weeks.

items.explanation: It is one of ATA 2026's few high-certainty recommendations: treating mild subclinical disease diagnosed after the first trimester brings no benefit; ASRM 2024 does not recommend treating subclinical disease in pregnant women either.

items.stem: A woman with Graves' disease controlled on methimazole (fictional case) wants to try to conceive. According to ATA 2026, what is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep methimazole throughout pregnancy.
options.why: ATA recommends switching to propylthiouracil when planning pregnancy; continuing methimazole is reserved for when propylthiouracil is unavailable or contraindicated.

options.text: Switch to propylthiouracil while planning pregnancy.
options.why: Correct: strong recommendation with moderate certainty (Recommendations Table 14).

options.text: Radioactive iodine and try to conceive the following month.
options.why: After radioactive iodine, ATA advises deferring pregnancy for at least six months.

options.text: Stop the antithyroid drug and monitor.
options.why: Overt hyperthyroidism should be treated before conception (GPS).

items.explanation: ATA also asks for a discussion with the patient of the risks and benefits of each option (antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, surgery) and their timelines to conception.

items.title: Case: Rocío, Martín and a TSH of 5.4 before IVF

steps.text: Rocío (fictional case), 37, and Martín have been trying to conceive for 2 years and IVF is indicated. Rocío has no thyroid symptoms and regular cycles. ATA 2026 and ETA 2021 order TSH for every woman with infertility; NICE NG257 would only order it with symptoms. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

TSH 5.4 mU/L, normal free T4, positive TPOAb. Her age and the scheduled IVF impose a time constraint, and with positive TPOAb normalisation is unlikely: ATA considers it sensible to offer low-dose levothyroxine (25–75 mcg/day) straight away through shared decision-making, and ETA recommends treating TSH > 4.0 to < 2.5. ASRM 2024 would not recommend treatment. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]] [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]]

After discussing it, Rocío starts 50 mcg/day. After 4–6 weeks TSH is 1.9 mU/L, within the 0.5–2.5 target. ATA suggests one TSH within the 6–12 weeks before stimulation and avoiding testing during stimulation or within 2 weeks of the trigger. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]

The pregnancy test is positive. Because her hypothyroidism is subclinical, ATA notes that there are no data supporting a standard 25% dose increase on confirming pregnancy: it proposes a small increase (e.g., 12.5 mcg/day) or adjusting according to TSH, which is checked about 2 weeks after the positive test and then every 4 weeks in the first half. Rocío asks about selenium “for the antibodies”: ATA advises against offering it to antibody-positive pregnant women. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]

asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.title: Subclinical hypothyroidism in the infertile female population: a guideline
asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.population: Women with infertility or miscarriage and pregnant women, in relation to subclinical hypothyroidism. Replaces the 2015 ASRM version.
asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.finding: Use the laboratory TSH cut-offs; if unavailable, 4.12 mIU/L for non-pregnant women and those attempting pregnancy (B; moderate). Counsel that subclinical hypothyroidism and a TSH of 2.5–4.0 mIU/L are not associated with more miscarriage (B; moderate). Treating subclinical hypothyroidism with levothyroxine in women desiring pregnancy or pregnant is not recommended (B; moderate). Test TSH and T4 when there are signs or symptoms of hypothyroidism (including irregular cycles), not in all infertility patients (B; moderate). Do not screen asymptomatic women for thyroid autoimmunity; it may be considered in recurrent pregnancy loss (C; weak).
asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.limitations: Full PDF read (Fertil Steril 2024;121:765-82). Strength of evidence A/B/C and strength of recommendation strong/moderate/weak. Much of its position rests on an influential trial having data-integrity concerns. US context.

ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.title: American Thyroid Association 2026 Guidelines for Thyroid Disease in Preconception, Pregnancy, and Postpartum
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.authors: Korevaar TIM, Leung AM, Alexander EK, Bliddal S, Boelaert K, Brenta G, Chou R, Dhillon-Smith R, Dosiou C, Eaton JL, Guan H, Kilpatrick SJ, Lasserre BJ, Lee SY, Maraka S, Meister KD, Morris-Wiseman LF, Nguyen CT, Pearce EN, Shan Z
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.population: Women planning pregnancy (including those with infertility, recurrent miscarriage or fertility treatment), pregnant women and women postpartum or breastfeeding. Replaces the 2017 ATA guideline; endorsed by, among others, ESHRE, the European Thyroid Association, ACOG, the Endocrine Society and the Latin American Thyroid Society.
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.finding: Infertility: TSH for all women with infertility or recurrent miscarriage (GPS) and optional TPOAb (conditional, low); on levothyroxine, target TSH 0.5–2.5 mU/L (GPS). Subclinical hypothyroidism: confirm after 4–6 weeks (conditional, moderate); TSH > 10 mU/L, treat (GPS); if persistent, low-dose levothyroxine (25–75 mcg/day; 25–50 in flowchart 1) (conditional, low certainty). Euthyroid autoimmunity (TPOAb and/or TgAb): do not offer levothyroxine (strong, high), recheck TSH and FT4 every 3–6 months; no prednisolone or immunoglobulin. Pregnancy: without a laboratory-specific interval, TSH 0.1–4.0 mU/L in the first and second trimesters. Iodine: 250 mcg/day total intake in pregnancy and lactation (strong, moderate); 150 mcg/day supplement in women at risk of deficiency (conditional, moderate); avoid > 500 mcg/day. Do not offer selenium to euthyroid antibody-positive pregnant women (conditional, moderate).
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.limitations: Full text read in the published version deposited in the University of California repository (eScholarship). Recommendations carry no individual number: they are cited by their “Recommendations Table” and page. Strength strong (“should”) or conditional (“may”), GRADE certainty very low to high, or good practice statement (GPS). The authors acknowledge that much of the evidence is of low or moderate quality; dissenting comments from group members are in supplementary material that was not reviewed. It gives no data specific to Argentina or Spain.

eshre-2022-rpl.title: ESHRE guideline: recurrent pregnancy loss: an update in 2022
eshre-2022-rpl.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on RPL; Bender Atik R, Christiansen OB, Elson J, et al.
eshre-2022-rpl.population: Couples with recurrent pregnancy loss (two or more losses).
eshre-2022-rpl.finding: Low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent loss in unexplained RPL (strong); do not use high doses without hyperhomocysteinaemia or conditions raising NTD risk (diabetes, epilepsy). Prophylactic vitamin D may be considered in preconception counselling (GPP) although evidence of effectiveness is absent; vitamin D testing to find a cause is not recommended. Multivitamins: advise options safe in pregnancy (GPP); they are not a treatment.
eshre-2022-rpl.limitations: Recommendations table and vitamin D chapter read in the full ESHRE PDF. Specific RPL population; several recommendations are good practice points (GPP), not trial-based.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

eta-2021-thyroid-art.title: 2021 European Thyroid Association Guideline on Thyroid Disorders prior to and during Assisted Reproduction
eta-2021-thyroid-art.authors: Poppe K, Bisschop P, Fugazzola L, Minziori G, Unuane D, Weghofer A
eta-2021-thyroid-art.population: Women and men in subfertile couples, before and during assisted reproduction (IVF/ICSI), in the European context. Aimed at endocrinologists and gynaecologists.
eta-2021-thyroid-art.finding: Screen TSH and TPOAb in every woman seeking advice for subfertility (R1; 1, ØØØO); TgAb if TSH > 2.5 mIU/L with negative TPOAb (R2). Defines subclinical hypothyroidism as TSH > 4.0 mIU/L or above the assay upper limit if that is higher; treat with levothyroxine to keep TSH < 2.5 mIU/L, with or without autoimmunity (R12, R13; 1, ØØOO). With autoimmunity and TSH between 2.5 and 4.0, low-dose levothyroxine (25–50 µg) case by case (R15; 2, ØØOO). Do not systematically treat euthyroid women with autoimmunity undergoing IVF/ICSI (R19; 2, ØØOO). Check TSH after stimulation in women with autoimmunity on levothyroxine (R17).
eta-2021-thyroid-art.limitations: Full text read on the PubMed Central HTML page (no pagination). Grades: 1 = strong recommendation, 2 = weak or suggestion; ØOOO very low to ØØØØ high quality. It predates ATA 2026 and the T4LIFE trial (2022), although it already includes TABLET and the Chinese IVF trial; its thresholds and its case-by-case levothyroxine stance in euthyroid autoimmunity differ from later guidelines.

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse.
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.
